<problem>
For each \(q\in\{5,7,9,11\}\), let \(K=\mathbb F_{q^2}\) and regard \(V=K^2\) as a four-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb F_q\). The points and lines of \(PG(V)\) are its one-dimensional and two-dimensional \(\mathbb F_q\)-subspaces, respectively. Define
\[
J(\infty)=\{(0,x):x\in K\},\qquad J(k)=\{(x,kx):x\in K\}\quad(k\in K),
\]
and fix the spread \(\mathcal S_q=\{J(k):k\in K\cup\{\infty\}\}\). Here a spread is a collection of projective lines partitioning the projective points.

A regulus is a set \(R\) of \(q+1\) pairwise disjoint projective lines such that every projective line meeting three members of \(R\) meets all its members. Its opposite regulus \(R^{\mathrm{opp}}\) is the set of projective lines meeting every member of \(R\).

A connected \(t\)-nest in \(\mathcal S_q\) is a set \(N\) of \(t\) distinct reguli contained in \(\mathcal S_q\) satisfying both of the following conditions:
* Every line of \(\mathcal S_q\) belongs to either zero or exactly two members of \(N\).
* The graph whose vertices are the members of \(N\), with two vertices adjacent when the corresponding reguli share a line, is connected.

Call \(N\) hemi-replaceable if, for every \(R\in N\), one can choose a subset \(H_R\subseteq R^{\mathrm{opp}}\) of size \((q+1)/2\) such that
\[
\left(\mathcal S_q\setminus\bigcup_{R\in N}R\right)\cup\bigcup_{R\in N}H_R
\]
is a spread. Two nests are equivalent if an invertible semilinear transformation of the \(\mathbb F_q\)-vector space \(V\), acting projectively and preserving \(\mathcal S_q\) setwise, maps one nest onto the other.

Let \(a_{q,t}\) be the number of equivalence classes of connected \(t\)-nests in \(\mathcal S_q\) that are not hemi-replaceable. For commuting indeterminates \(X,Y\), determine the exact polynomial
\[
F(X,Y)=\sum_{q\in\{5,7,9,11\}}\sum_{t=1}^{q}a_{q,t}X^qY^t.
\]
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer is the exact polynomial F(X,Y), with every nonzero coefficient explicitly specified and all omitted coefficients understood to be zero. Equivalently, it is a complete table of the exact integers a_{q,t} for every q in {5,7,9,11} and every t from 1 to q.

9	## 1. Reguli as circles
10	
11	Identify the spread lines with
12	\[
13	\Omega=K\cup\{\infty\}.
14	\]
15	The reguli contained in the spread are precisely the images of
16	\[
17	C_0=\mathbb F_q\cup\{\infty\}
18	\]

21	Here is a direct justification. Map three members of a regulus to \(J(0),J(1),J(\infty)\). Their common transversals are
22	\[
23	T_z=\left\langle (z,0),(0,z)\right\rangle_{\mathbb F_q},
24	\qquad z\in K^*/\mathbb F_q^*.
25	\]
26	The spread lines meeting every \(T_z\) are exactly \(J(k)\), \(k\in C_0\). Thus the three members determine the regulus uniquely, and the asserted description follows.
27	
28	For computation, all circles are generated by
29	\[
30	\{z\in K:(z-a)^{q+1}=r\},
31	\quad a\in K,\quad r\in\mathbb F_q^*,
32	\tag{1}
33	\]
34	and
35	\[
36	(a+b\mathbb F_q)\cup\{\infty\},
37	\quad a\in K,\quad b\in K^*.
38	\tag{2}
39	\]
40	Indeed, the norm-one circle is a Baer subline: for \(\alpha\notin\mathbb F_q\), use
41	\[
42	s\longmapsto\frac{s-\alpha}{s-\alpha^q},
43	\qquad s\in\mathbb F_q\cup\{\infty\}.
44	\]
45	Translations and dilations give (1), while (2) is immediate.

50	\]

52	\[
53	\frac{|PGL(2,q^2)|}{|PGL(2,q)|},
54	\]
55	so the list is exhaustive. Distinct circles intersect in at most two points. The program additionally checks that every three-element subset of \(\Omega\) lies in exactly one generated circle.
56	
57	In this language, a nest is a connected collection of circles in which each point occurs zero or twice.
58	
59	## 2. The exact hemi-replaceability test
60	
61	Put \(m=q+1\), and fix a generator \(g\) of \(K^*\).
62	
63	For each circle \(C\), choose a matrix \(A_C\in GL(2,K)\) taking \(C_0\) to \(C\). Its opposite-regulus lines are
64	\[
65	T_{C,i}=g^iA_C(\mathbb F_q^2),
66	\qquad i\in\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z.
67	\tag{3}
68	\]
69	For \(p\in C\), write the vector representing its intersection with \(A_C(\mathbb F_q^2)\) as
70	\[
71	d_{C,p}(1,p),
72	\]
73	using \((0,1)\) at infinity, and let
74	\[
75	s_{C,p}=\log_g(d_{C,p})\pmod m.
76	\]
77	Only the coset of \(d_{C,p}\) modulo \(\mathbb F_q^*\) matters.
78	
79	For two circles \(C,D\) sharing \(p\), the lines \(T_{C,i}\) and \(T_{D,j}\) intersect precisely when
80	\[
81	j=i+s_{C,p}-s_{D,p}\pmod m.
82	\tag{4}
83	\]
84	
85	Construct a graph \(\Gamma_N\) with vertices \((C,i)\), for \(C\in N\) and \(i\in\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\), and edges given by (4). Selecting opposite-regulus lines is therefore equivalent to assigning a Boolean value to every vertex. The replacement is a spread exactly when adjacent vertices receive complementary values and every circle has \(m/2\) selected vertices.
86	
87	For the range in this question, the latter condition is automatic:
88	
89	**Lemma.** If \(N\) is connected and \(|N|\le q\), then \(N\) is hemi-replaceable if and only if \(\Gamma_N\) is bipartite.
90	
91	**Proof.** Necessity follows from (4).
92	
93	For sufficiency, first consider the multigraph on the circles, with one edge for each shared point. It is connected and has degree \(q+1\) at every vertex, with at most two parallel edges. If it were bipartite, each part would have at least \((q+1)/2\) vertices, forcing \(|N|\ge q+1\). Thus it has an odd closed walk based at every circle.
94	
95	Lifting such a walk to \(\Gamma_N\) sends
96	\[
97	(C,i)\longmapsto(C,i+\delta)
98	\]
99	for some fixed \(\delta\), independently of \(i\). In any proper two-colouring, these endpoints have opposite colours. Summing over all \(i\) shows that each colour occurs exactly \(m/2\) times above \(C\).
100	
101	Thus a bipartition selects the required half of every opposite regulus. Equation (4) makes the selections complementary on every shared spread line. These shared lines contain all points of the removed part of the spread, so the resulting lines form a spread. ∎
102	
103	This test permits arbitrary halves of the opposite reguli; it does **not** restrict the search to a special kind of half-regulus.
104	
105	## 3. Equivalence group
106	
107	The group induced on \(\Omega\) by the transformations in the question is exactly
108	\[
109	P\Gamma L(2,q^2).
110	\tag{5}
111	\]
112	
113	For completeness, normalize a spread-preserving semilinear transformation so that it fixes the two coordinate \(K\)-lines and their diagonal. After removing an extension of its automorphism of \(\mathbb F_q\), it has the form
114	\[
115	(x,y)\longmapsto(f(x),f(y)).
116	\]
117	Preservation of every \(K\)-line gives
118	\[
119	f(kx)=\phi(k)f(x).
120	\]
121	Normalizing \(f(1)=1\) shows that \(f\) is additive and multiplicative, hence a field automorphism of \(K\). Undoing the normalization proves (5). Conversely, all transformations in (5) are allowed.
122	
123	The setwise stabilizer \(G_0\) of \(C_0\) consists of \(PGL(2,q)\) together with all automorphisms of \(K\). If \(q=p^e\), its order is
124	\[
125	|G_0|=2e\,q(q^2-1).
126	\tag{6}
127	\]
128	
129	The program first canonicalizes under \(G_0\). It then removes the distinguished circle: for each circle \(C\) of a nest, it maps \(C\) to \(C_0\) and canonicalizes again. These are all possible rootings. Two nests are equivalent if and only if their sets of canonical rootings coincide.
130	
131	## 4. Why the search is exhaustive
132	
133	By transitivity on circles, require the nest to contain \(C_0\).
134	
135	During the search:
136	
137	* \(O\) is the set of points currently covered once;
138	* points already covered twice are forbidden to every further circle;
139	* \(A\) is the set of circles still allowed.
140	
141	Choose a point \(p\in O\), and branch over circles in \(A\) containing \(p\). Any completion must contain exactly one of these circles. Every added circle meets the current collection, so the output is connected. If \(O\) becomes empty, a connected completion cannot contain any further circle.
142	
143	If \(r\) circles remain available in the size bound, every selected circle must have at most \(2r\) open points. Also, any future circle \(D\) must satisfy
144	\[
145	|D\cap O|\ge q+1-2(r-1).
146	\tag{7}
147	\]
148	Both bounds follow because distinct circles intersect in at most two points.
149	
150	There is also safe symmetry pruning. At each node the maintained group preserves the selected circles and \(A\). Restrict it to fix the chosen open point, and branch on candidate orbits. After exploring representative \(D\), remove its entire orbit from subsequent sibling branches. A completion using another member of that orbit maps to a completion already covered by the representative branch. In the recursive branch only \(D\), not its whole orbit, is excluded.
151	
152	These observations prove inductively that every connected nest of size at most \(q\) is represented in the search output.
153

136	* points already covered twice are forbidden to every further circle;
137	* \(A\) is the set of circles still allowed.
138	
139	Choose a point \(p\in O\), and branch over circles in \(A\) containing \(p\). Any completion must contain exactly one of these circles. Every added circle meets the current collection, so the output is connected. If \(O\) becomes empty, a connected completion cannot contain any further circle.
140	
141	If \(r\) circles remain available in the size bound, every selected circle must have at most \(2r\) open points. Also, any future circle \(D\) must satisfy
142	\[
143	|D\cap O|\ge q+1-2(r-1).
144	\tag{7}
145	\]
146	Both bounds follow because distinct circles intersect in at most two points.
147	
148	There is also safe symmetry pruning. At each node the maintained group preserves the selected circles and \(A\). Restrict it to fix the chosen open point, and branch on candidate orbits. After exploring representative \(D\), remove its entire orbit from subsequent sibling branches. A completion using another member of that orbit maps to a completion already covered by the representative branch. In the recursive branch only \(D\), not its whole orbit, is excluded.
149	
150	These observations prove inductively that every connected nest of size at most \(q\) is represented in the search output.
